opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to be a hybrid, and the interesting question is where you draw the line. The way I like to think about it is by analogy to how people work. There's fast, reactive control, like keeping your balance or adjusting your grip when an object slips, and that has to happen locally because you just can't tolerate the latency or the unreliability of a network round trip. If your Wi-Fi drops while the robot is holding a glass of water, it can't just freeze or drop it. So that low-level, high-frequency loop has to live on the robot.

But a lot of the more deliberative stuff, like figuring out what to do next, interpreting a complicated instruction, or reasoning about a situation it hasn't seen before, can tolerate a bit more latency. That's where you could imagine leaning on a much bigger model running somewhere else. It's a little like how you might stop and think, or even call someone and ask, when you're stuck on a hard problem, but you don't call anyone to keep yourself from tripping.

For affordability this matters a lot, because the compute you put on the robot is a real cost, and it also costs you in power and heat. If every robot needs a top-end GPU onboard, that sets a floor on the price. So I think the architectures that will make sense are ones where you have a reasonably capable but efficient model on the device, handling the moment-to-moment behavior and maintaining safety, and then something larger that can be consulted more sparingly for higher-level guidance.

The tricky part, and I think this is still an open research problem, is making these pieces work together gracefully: how the onboard system degrades sensibly when the remote part is slow or unavailable, and how you train the whole thing so the division of labor emerges naturally rather than being hand-engineered. I'd be wary of drawing that boundary too rigidly by hand, because historically in this field, whenever we've imposed a lot of hand-designed structure, learning-based approaches eventually found a better way to split things up.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger remote model can provide higher-level guidance and that the onboard system should degrade gracefully when the remote part is slow or unavailable, implying stronger deliberative capability with better connectivity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what the robot is doing, but there's a pretty clear structure that falls out once you think about what actually needs to be fast versus what needs to be smart.

The things that have to run onboard are the things with tight latency requirements. Low-level control, the stuff that's closing the loop at tens or hundreds of hertz, the reflexes, basic safety behaviors. If the robot is about to knock a glass off a table, you don't want that decision to depend on a round trip to a data center. And honestly, those components don't need to be enormous. A lot of the low-level motor control can be handled by relatively small networks, and that's getting cheaper every year.

Then there's a layer above that, which is the perception and the policy, the thing that's actually looking at the scene and deciding what to do over the next second or two. That's where it gets interesting, because the trend with these foundation models for robotics is that bigger models are just better. They generalize more, they're more robust to weird situations, they understand language better. So there's a real tension. You want a big model, but you don't want a big computer on a robot that's supposed to cost a few thousand dollars.

And I think the answer there is probably not one or the other, it's an asymmetric split. You have something like a small, fast model onboard that can act competently on its own for a little while, and then a larger model that's offboard, in the cloud or on a local server, that's providing higher-level guidance. The big model is doing the semantic reasoning, the long-horizon planning, figuring out what the task even is, and it's sending down something more abstract, like a subgoal or a latent instruction. The small model is turning that into actual motor commands. If the connection drops for a second, the small model keeps going on its last instruction. It degrades gracefully instead of freezing.

What's nice about that is the big model can be shared. One large model can serve a whole fleet, and that's where the economics get really favorable, because then the marginal cost of the intelligence is small per robot. The robot itself can be cheap. It's a little like how your phone works, right? It does a lot locally, but the heavy stuff goes elsewhere.

The other thing I'd say, which people sometimes miss, is that the external system isn't just for inference. The really valuable part of having robots connected is the data. Every robot out there is collecting experience, and that experience goes back to improve the shared model, and then the improvements get pushed to every robot. That flywheel is the thing that I think matters most in the long run. So I'd actually argue that an affordable robot should be designed from the start assuming it's part of a fleet that's learning collectively, not as a standalone device that happens to have a network connection.

Where I'd push back a bit on the pure cloud vision is that I don't think you want the robot to be helpless without connectivity. Partly for the latency and safety reasons, but also because the embodied experience is really local. The robot has to deal with what's right in front of it, right now, and there's something a little off about a design where that depends on infrastructure that's hundreds of miles away. So onboard should be competent and the offboard should make it smart, rather than onboard being dumb and offboard being everything.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an offboard larger model provides higher-level reasoning and guidance, while the onboard model continues on its last instruction if connectivity drops. This communicates that stronger connectivity enables more capable behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the natural architecture is a hierarchy, where the things that need to happen very quickly happen onboard, and the things that can tolerate some latency can happen remotely. You don’t want the robot to need a round trip to a data center to keep its balance or respond when it makes contact with something. But deciding how to approach a task, or interpreting a complicated instruction, could use a much larger model running somewhere else.

The interesting question is where you draw that boundary. You could imagine the remote system giving instructions like, “Go pick up that cup,” but the onboard system still has to be quite capable to execute that reliably. It needs to respond to what it sees, adjust its grasp, and handle small surprises without asking for help at every step.

So I wouldn’t think of an affordable robot as just a body connected to a brain in the cloud. I’d think of it as having enough local intelligence to act competently, with access to more computation when it needs to deliberate. And that division might change depending on the task: something familiar can run almost entirely locally, while an unfamiliar situation warrants calling out to a more capable system.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot can use remote computation for some tasks, but does not say its cognitive capability improves as Internet connection quality improves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful distinction is between things that have to happen quickly and things that can tolerate some delay. If the robot is balancing, or making contact with an object, you really want that control loop to run onboard. You don’t want the robot to fall over because your Wi-Fi connection dropped.

But if it’s figuring out how to accomplish a task, or interpreting a fairly complicated instruction, that computation could happen remotely. You could have a much larger model that provides guidance, and a smaller onboard model that turns that guidance into actions.

The interesting question is how much autonomy that smaller model needs. I would want it to be capable enough that, if the connection goes away, it can finish the immediate motion or stop safely. The external system can help it make better decisions, but it shouldn’t be necessary for every single action.

And affordability doesn’t automatically mean moving everything to the cloud. Communication has costs, inference has costs, and you might be running this robot all day. So I suspect the practical answer is a mixture: a fairly capable local policy, with more expensive computation available when the robot encounters something that actually requires it.

r001.rationale: The response says remote computation can provide guidance and onboard autonomy should handle connection loss, but it does not say the robot becomes smarter as Internet connectivity improves.
